lecture_title: AST 102: The Life of a Star

slides.title: AST 102: The Life of a Star
body_text: Birth, main sequence, death
Dr. Alex Morgan
slides.speaker_notes: Sky report, then: stars are not eternal. Today is their biography.

slides.title: Luminosity and Temperature
body_text: Luminosity: total power output, in units of the Sun's
Temperature: from color or spectral class
Luminosity needs distance plus apparent brightness
slides.speaker_notes: Parallax and magnitudes from last week feed straight into this.

slides.title: The Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram
body_text: Luminosity on the vertical axis
Temperature on the horizontal axis, increasing to the left
Main sequence: a diagonal band holding about 90 percent of stars
Giants upper right, white dwarfs lower left
slides.speaker_notes: Build it on the wall with star cards. The main sequence appears by itself.

slides.title: Main Sequence Means Hydrogen Fusion
body_text: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores
A star's mass sets its place on the main sequence
Stars stay in nearly the same spot for most of their lives
slides.speaker_notes: Common mistake: stars do not slide down the main sequence as they age.

slides.title: Fusion in Brief
body_text: Core temperature in the Sun: about 15 million K
Four hydrogen nuclei combine into one helium nucleus
The helium has about 0.7 percent less mass; that mass becomes energy
The Sun converts about 600 million tons of hydrogen every second
slides.speaker_notes: A chemical fire the size of the Sun would burn out in thousands of years. Fusion lasts billions.

slides.title: Hydrostatic Equilibrium
body_text: Gravity pulls inward
Pressure from hot gas pushes outward
Balanced, so the star keeps a steady size
slides.speaker_notes: A balloon squeezed between two hands: squeeze and push back in balance.

slides.title: Mass and Lifetime
body_text: Lifetime is roughly 10 billion years x (mass in Suns) to the power -2.5
A 10-solar-mass star lives a few tens of millions of years
A 0.5-solar-mass red dwarf lives more than 50 billion years
slides.speaker_notes: More fuel, but a much bigger engine. The gas-guzzler runs out first.

slides.title: Red Giants
body_text: Core hydrogen runs out; the core contracts and heats
Hydrogen fuses in a shell around the core
The outer layers swell and cool: a red giant
The Sun will do this in about 5 billion years
slides.speaker_notes: The Sun will swell to roughly the size of Earth's orbit. Earth may or may not survive.

slides.title: Endings for Low-Mass Stars
body_text: Below about 8 solar masses
The outer layers drift off as a planetary nebula
The core remains as a white dwarf, about the size of Earth
slides.speaker_notes: Planetary nebulas have nothing to do with planets. Old telescopes made them look like planet disks.

slides.title: Endings for High-Mass Stars
body_text: Above about 8 solar masses: core collapse and a supernova
Remnant: a neutron star, about 20 km across
The most massive stars, roughly above 20 solar masses, leave black holes
Supernovae scatter heavy elements into space
slides.speaker_notes: The mass limits are approximate and still debated. The iron in your blood came from stars like these.
